name: 1 - Why Public Engagement? Transcript
content:
Beth S. Noveck: is one of…
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Danielle is one of the preeminent political philosophers of our time. We'll put some links to her books in the chat and to her bio. She's written many, many books. I think relevant, particularly for this conversation, is a recent volume that she edited, From Voice to Influence, Understanding Citizenship in the Digital Age, published by Chicago Press, and most recently, Justice by Means of Democracy.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: which I think very much provides the ideological foundation for the conversation we're going to have about participatory democracy. But Danielle is much more than just a scholar, or in addition, not just a scholar, but also a scholar. She is very much a practitioner and an advocate who has been studying and practicing and advocating for reconnecting people to their civic power.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: to governance, and that's what we're here to do today. This is a revamp, if you will, or a renovation, to steal a term that Danielle uses so eloquently, of a lecture series many of you have attended called the Reboot Democracy Lecture Series, for a number of years, but we're doing this not as a series of lectures, but as a series of workshops. We're going to hear from leading practitioners, from
 
 Beth S. Noveck: doers, some of whom I see, coming into the room who are here with us now.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So we can explore together what does AI mean for this democratic age, and how might we do democracy and do participatory democracy better than we have done before. I've listed this as 11 plus workshops. The plus is because I'm hoping we're gonna add more. And if you're in the room and you have experience and expertise to share, if something is working where you
 
 Beth S. Noveck: we'd love to hear from you, and we'd love for you to participate. So please, do share your expertise now, get in touch with us, and use the chat to tell us who's here. So Danielle and I are going to have a bit of a conversation over the next half hour, and then open it up to your contributions, questions, suggestions, and engagement after that. Please do sign up.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: For upcoming workshops, we'll put the link in the chat as well for the whole series, and you can sign up for some of the workshops that are coming up. One last logistical note before we dive into the substance. This session is being recorded, as Zoom has already told you, but we will turn off the recording during the Q&A. We do that so that we can have a frank conversation. We have a lot of people, particularly in government here.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: We want you to feel comfortable
 
 Beth S. Noveck: that no question is too frivolous to ask, no question is too small, about how we can actually do things differently. Please right-click on your own square to rename yourselves. If you're not appearing with your name, if you'd like to add your institution and where you're coming from, we'd love to know who's here. And we encourage you also to use the chat to have a conversation. Even as Danielle and I are talking, there's so many experts
 
 Beth S. Noveck: here in the room. Please do use the chat to have a conversation, but use the Q&A button at the bottom of your screen.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: You'll see it, fourth in from the right, if you would like to ask a question, or sort of formally contribute to the conversation, so that we can organize that conversation later.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And finally, my colleagues have asked me to note to please mute yourself during the conversation so we can all hear one another, rather than hearing your phone ringing in the background.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Okay, with that, any logistical items that I've forgotten?
 
 Agueda Quiroga (InnovateUS): Absolutely nothing. Perfect.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Okay, I'm gonna share the… if I can, should I hit share results so we can see who's here? Am I allowed to… can… I think that should work.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: But tell me if I've done something wrong with the poll. I'm gonna get us started and say… just offer a few words by way of intro. Danielle is going to do the same, and then we're gonna have a bit of a conversation with one another, and then, as I said, open it up to… to conversation with you. So I very much got my start in this world of participatory democracy, especially enabled by technology.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And Danielle, I don't know if you know this, but back in 1999, I started a company with the political philosopher Ben Barber.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So whatever one thinks of starting a company with a political philosophy will help to explain why I'm a professor and not the CEO of a software company. You know, maybe from a commercial perspective, it wasn't all that helpful. But it was a tremendously exciting endeavor, because we worked together to translate many of the ideas that he had been writing about, about stronger democracy.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: back in the early 80s, and what it could mean to reinvigorate participation in our society for the era of the web.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: We were really excited, and Ben, story for another time about how Ben drove our graphic designers crazy, trying to redraw the Athenian pnex on the screen of the then fledgling World Wide Web, which was not so easy to do.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Our aim at the time, though, was to do more than just enable conversation for its own sake. We didn't… we wanted people to be able to have conversations, but we wanted to connect those conversations to power.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: We wanted to reinvigorate the kind of experimental institutions that grew up in Athenian democracy, where citizens could actively shape decisions in their community.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And I think those early days were really heady times for all of us, who worked in what we used to call e-democracy in those days. We saw the web as being really potentially quite transformative.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: But fast forward, and I would argue, with some degree of self-flagellation and hand-wringing, that even though the number and variety of platforms have grown, and we've seen tremendous, and I think each of us have participated in a lot of experiments.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Many of which have been successful.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: that I don't think…
 
 Beth S. Noveck: the promise has fulfilled itself, despite the technology that we all have at our fingertips. I think the hope that we had
 
 Beth S. Noveck: that institutions would incorporate, as your colleagues Glenn Weil and Audrey Tang have right, that institutions would incorporate participation into the fabric of how they work.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: hasn't realized itself in practice. And I think what's happening in the news and the rising tide of violence, especially in America, is only further evidence of the frustration that people feel with the inability to participate in governance and the inability to essentially wield power over the decisions that matter in their lives.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So we've seen tremendous proliferation of tools, of experiments, of efforts to engage people in deliberation.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: But the reality is that so many of these tools have led to, what, what Ann Applebaum refers to as the dumpster fire of our democracy that is social media.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: But not the great promise of participatory democracy that we have hoped for.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: However.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: I think AI potentially could be a game changer. So what I'm hoping we're going to discuss today, and again, this is meant to be a very practical conversation aimed at our colleagues, particularly in government institutions.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: About how we might do things differently with AI, and whether AI could really help us, to realize the vision that, Ben had at the time, that we could use new technology.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: To really reinvigorate our participatory democracy and do things differently. So, I'm hoping today we're going to talk about what some of these challenges are to realizing a more participatory vision for how we govern.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Why we haven't solved the problems up until now, and to have a bit of a conversation together and with everyone in the room about whether and how we think AI
 
 Beth S. Noveck: could be a game changer or not, whether we're totally wrong and what we have to do differently, both in terms of our technology and in terms of our institutions. So let me stop there and pass it to you, and I'm going to ask my colleagues, I don't know if everybody, if I can take this poll off the screen so we can see Danielle better.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: But hopefully you can chime in, and hopefully the polls…
 
 Danielle Allen : Here we go. Let me pass… my screen, so that works. Perfect.
 
 Danielle Allen : Beth, first, let me just say how exciting it is that our two labs are collaborating on this series. We're so grateful to you for your openness and adaptability in being interested in, you know, reimagining, renovating this webinar series.
 
 Georg Diez: We're excited to partner with you on it, and we agree with you, it couldn't be more important.
 
 Danielle Allen : So, I'm glad 11 plus will be working on that plus, and trying to make sure that what we're doing is supporting a community of practice that really is at the leading edge of helping us all renovate our democratic institutions more generally, so that we can secure healthy communities.
 
 Danielle Allen : I love your story about Ben. I did not know that you tried to start a company with Ben Barber in the 1990s, and that sort of explains a lot, too, of how the two of us have connected, have that synergy. I mean, he was a great, of course. I learned a lot from him in his arguments about stronger democracy.
 
 Danielle Allen : It's funny, in that same time period, when you were working on that, I was in Chicago working on place-based local democracy. No tech involved. People in places doing things with each other. I was a relatively young assistant professor at the University of Chicago.
 
 Danielle Allen : I also had visions of Athens in my head. I had spent a lot of time studying ancient Athenian democracy. There was an incredibly empowered citizenry. They were very good at
 
 Danielle Allen : Moving knowledge through the community, and also at building kind of cross-cutting kinds of connections so that the different constituencies in the city were really feeding together, mixing things up, bridging, and forming a really kind of connected, societal fabric.
 
 Danielle Allen : at any rate, I had landed in Chicago, and I had realized that the city of Chicago, you know, and the sort of the south side where I was, was about the same scale as ancient Athens, and so I thought, well, if they could do it, you know, in ancient Athens, if we considered democracy in a really place-based way in America, we could really bring new energy to sort of lots of nodes of democracy around the country, and build from place out to a healthier democracy.
 
 Danielle Allen : I tell that story because I think that, actually, the moment that we're in is precisely one where the opportunity is to bring place and technology together.
 
 Danielle Allen : I think the early movement of bringing tech into democracy wasn't very oriented to place. There was a sense that tech let us open up to sort of global context, global networks.
 
 Danielle Allen : And it wasn't always grounded in the kind of use case of specific social and political communities. I was really, you know, trying hard in the 90s to hold tech at bay, so I'm sort of the opposite of you. I was not a person who jumped in with both feet. Instead, I kept saying, no, no, no, no, I'm doing this real democracy thing with real people in real places.
 
 Danielle Allen : And over the last decade, of course, all of my friends in the technology space have been, you know, started banging me over the head with a club and saying, you know, Danielle, you're completely missing the boat. If you can't see how technology is going to transform everything we do, including politics, then you're never going to be able to actually build a healthy democracy that you care about.
 
 Danielle Allen : So that is what brought me into the technology conversation, the recognition that, indeed, technology is transforming what we can do in all of our institutions. And so I agree with Beth, I do think that the arrival of AI is potentially a game changer.
 
 Danielle Allen : And I think the real question is how we harness it for core Healthy Democracy goals. Again, for me, harnessing it is about putting place and technology together. That's why this series is so exciting. So many of you are working on healthy governance in specific places.
 
 Danielle Allen : So I want to say two more words about healthy governance and the opportunity that we have to upgrade our representative institutions so that they can succeed in 21st century conditions.
 
 Nancy S: Hey, how are you? Hi, Gary.
 
 Danielle Allen : By succeed, I mean that they should be responsive to the people, and be felt as responsive, that there's a good, strong feedback loop, that they be effective in their decision making, and then also effective in implementation. And that also requires a reliance on design principles like transparency and accountability, alongside the principle of efficiency.
 
 Danielle Allen : But an important thing to say is that our representative institutions are, in some sense, sort of the spine of our society. And we can think of that spine as consisting of three vertebrae.
 
 Danielle Allen : First, there is citizen participation. That is a key aspect of representation, that people are able to funnel their points of view and perspectives into our shared decision-making mechanisms. Then the second vertebra is decision makers deciding.
 
 Danielle Allen : Whether those are elected officials or appointed, civil servants, people have to make some decisions. And then the third vertebrae is the implementation moment, and that can come either in the form of enforcement of regulations or in the delivery of services.
 
 Danielle Allen : Now, I believe our job here in 2025, headed into 2026, is essentially to give an upgrade to that spine of our society in our representative institutions by thinking about how technology can help us do the citizen participation piece better, help us do the decision-maker deciding piece better, and help us do implementation better. But the real trick is that you have to actually hook
 
 Danielle Allen : each of those vertebrae up together. So, we're gonna really focus on citizen participation in this webinar series.
 
 Danielle Allen : why it's important, how we can do better. We've got concrete examples, great work in Bowling Green, Kentucky, for example, where people have been using Polis and Google Jigsaw Sensemaker to elicit a broader range of opinion in the city, to find minority perspectives, to find points of consensus that weren't previously visible, and feed that all into the development of a 25-year plan for the city.
 
 Danielle Allen : Engage California is doing similar work, also seeking to improve the sense-making that supports decision-making.
 
 Danielle Allen : So we have a lot of concrete examples of how we can improve citizen participation, and one of the lessons I hope we'll pull out throughout the series is how we make sure that that gets hooked up
 
 Danielle Allen : to decision making, gets hooked up to implementation, so that there really is a feedback loop. That's where responsiveness comes from, and that's really one of the important criteria of success for citizen participation.
 
 Danielle Allen : So, I will stop there with that broad table setting, but I, like Beth, am just so grateful to all of you for giving of your time and energy and creativity to this incredibly important conversation.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And we have a lot of energy and creativity and expertise in the room. I see a number of the folks who you have name-checked actually hear. So I want to just offer a reminder to please use the chat. It will, to have a…
 
 Beth S. Noveck: what I call a conversation in four dimensions, put any questions, especially for Danielle, in the chat. But I want… and a plug to say that folks from Bowling Green and Jigsaw will be here as part of the series. The folks from the Design California Project will also be here, specifically to talk about what they've done and how they've done it.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And for our practitioners and our institution leaders, our decision makers and implementers in the room, all our speakers have been asked going forward to really talk about the how-tos of engagement. Very nitty-gritty, you know, don't be put off by the fact that this is being kicked off by two professors. We're gonna talk about how much it cost, how many people it took.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: how much time it took, what did you do first? What did you do second? Because ultimately, I think the goal here
 
 Beth S. Noveck: is for us to engender more engagement and more participation. And maybe, Danielle, let me just ask you a little bit about and tease out, I love the kind of three spines, idea and the connection between the engagement piece
 
 Beth S. Noveck: the decision-making and the implementation, just tease out a little bit more of those connections, and help us to understand it… I don't think it… why we do participation.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Because as obvious it may seem as the right thing to do, and a democratic nice-to-have.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: when we get busy and budgets get low, it always falls by the wayside, back to the why we haven't done it. So I think it does make sense, and it was on the menu for today, to really talk about and articulate more about what the different visions are for why we do it.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And do you think in this day and age, given what's going on in the world, are there reasons that are more important now than others for why to engage?
 
 Danielle Allen : I appreciate that, Beth, that question, and I also appreciate your, naming the fact that we kicked this off with two professors.
 
 Danielle Allen : the rest of the series will dive into the nitty-gritty, but your question is an invitation to zoom way out, honestly, right, to the question of why does civic participation matter anyway, and even, you know, especially now in the 21st century. So I'm going to take you up on the invitation to answer that.
 
 Danielle Allen : questions, so folks will have to bear with me for a little bit, as I truly am a political philosopher, here in this conversation.
 
 Danielle Allen : The simple fact of the matter is that democracy itself is a technology, okay?
 
 Danielle Allen : It was discovered in antiquity many, many, you know, long, long time ago. It disappeared again, it was rediscovered in the 18th century, when people glued the idea of democracy, that is, popular participation, together with the concept of representation.
 
 Danielle Allen : And it was gluing those two things together that permitted the sort of scaling up of popular participation.
 
 Danielle Allen : But then that leads to the question of, okay, well, what kind of discovery was this about popular participation? Why do we invest in it?
 
 Danielle Allen : And there's a few different things that this technology of participation delivers for us as a society.
 
 Danielle Allen : One, it delivers vastly improved information flows. And at the end of the day, all decision-making depends on the quality of the information flows into the decision. So, it's, you know, a big, complex apparatus
 
 Danielle Allen : For hoovering up as much information as there possibly is in society, so that we can make the best possible kind of decision.
 
 Danielle Allen : Now, you might say, well, but hey, like, AI can hoover up all that information now, like, why do we need participation to hoover up information?
 
 Danielle Allen : And there are a lot of reasons why AI can't replace what humans have.
 
 Danielle Allen : Not all of our knowledge is represented in data.
 
 Danielle Allen : So data is a tranche of what we all know and think and have learned and so forth, but it does not capture all of human experience and perspective. And so we would lose all of that if we only relied on data tools sort of scraping the web. So that's why we still need real people, and we need to activate the agency of real people as thinkers and contributors. So that's thing one, is the sort of knowledge power that comes from participation.
 
 Danielle Allen : Thing two is the issue of legitimacy.
 
 Danielle Allen : At the end of the day, any given society is stable, only to the degree that people support it. And that doesn't matter if you're an autocracy or a democracy. Autocracies get very, very weak if there is no strong sense of legitimacy or, you know, connection to the institutions. Often, autocracies depend on people feeling protected. So even in autocracies, there is a need for popular opinion to have some meaningful degree of
 
 Danielle Allen : Support for the institutions.
 
 Danielle Allen : Now, you look at all the possibilities, again, participation is actually the best way of achieving legitimacy. So, yes, you can sometimes generate decisions faster without participation, but they will be thinner and more brittle. They won't have sustainability. So, it's actually more efficient over the long term
 
 Danielle Allen : to build in popular participation so that the decisions have that sustained legitimacy behind them. So that's the second thing.
 
 Nancy Seng: Where do I go?
 
 Danielle Allen : The third kind of power that comes from participation, in some sense, this is almost the most important one for human beings, is just plain freedom, alright? It's freedom. Now, why is that the case?
 
 Danielle Allen : Because what participation is, is a counterweight to other kinds of power. So, again, you can have power concentrated in an executive, or you could have power concentrated in the market.
 
 Danielle Allen : And if you let power be concentrated there without the counterweight of popular participation, then at the end of the day, that erodes the sort of space for action for ordinary people. And that's not a fancy point, it's not a political point, it's the point that history teaches over and over and over again.
 
 Danielle Allen : If you want to protect the space for agency, for ordinary people, you have to have a counterweight to the other kinds of power that exist in society. So, information.
 
 Danielle Allen : Legitimacy and sustainability, and freedom, okay?
 
 Danielle Allen : Those are the things that we get from participation.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So, why have given, given that, why… first of all, do you agree or disagree with my assessment that we have not done as well as we could have and needed to? And what's your diagno… so let me… let me ask you that first, and then…
 
 Beth S. Noveck: If we think we've not done as well as we needed to or could have, given the tools at our disposal up until now, why not?
 
 Danielle Allen : Thank you, Beth.
 
 Danielle Allen : Thank you. These questions are great, I love these questions. So I said democracy's a technology, and it is. And we also have other technologies, and in the 90s, we invented the internet, for example, for starters.
 
 Danielle Allen : And so, a few things have happened. For starters, the technology of democracy that was invented in the 18th century.
 
 Danielle Allen : was not designed for contemporary conditions. At the most basic level, it was designed for a much slower information flow, and for an information flow that was fragmented by geographic dispersal.
 
 Danielle Allen : So, I won't bore people with the details, but it was literally designed in a way that was taking into account the kind of basic expectation that it would be hard for people to circulate knowledge other than through the clinical institutions.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And that condition has changed completely, and that destabilizes our existing institutions. Can I interrupt you just for one moment. Is there an audio issue? Can people hear?
 
 Kate Carter: I see a note in the chat about, and I see some thumbs up that people can't hear.
 
 Danielle Allen : Oh, no!
 
 Tom Asher: Clearly.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Okay, good. Keep going, sorry to interrupt.
 
 Danielle Allen : Okay, so all I was gonna say was…
 
 Danielle Allen : the 18th century technology that is democracy, now it's under pressure because of 21st century conditions. Simultaneously, we have some new technologies, and in the 90s, I think what happened was… so why didn't we take advantage of technology as well as we might have done, or why did we get into trouble?
 
 Danielle Allen : A, I think we didn't fully understand the specific vulnerabilities of the 18th century technology that is democracy, and therefore we didn't know how to correct for those vulnerabilities with new technologies. But B, I think the other thing we lost sight of
 
 Danielle Allen : is that as a technology, democracy is fundamentally a place-based technology, okay? Right? That's why we have districts.
 
 Danielle Allen : And it doesn't, you know, you're a city, and you've got wards, or you've got counties, or, you know, your state is divided into counties, and then the, you know, we've got congressional districts. Democracy is a place-based technology. And in the 90s, we really saw technology as not place-based.
 
 Danielle Allen : We saw it as enabling precisely all the things that didn't depend on place. And so there's all kinds of stuff we figured out that way. Social media took off because it didn't depend on place, and it… so we have new capacities, new ways of organizing ourselves.
 
 Danielle Allen : But now, I think the job is to recognize that democracy is a place-based technology, and to actually embed technology into helping that place-based technology work better.
 
 Danielle Allen : So, now, Beth, what do you think? Why do you think we didn't make more progress in the 90s?
 
 Beth S. Noveck: I think, so yes and. I think there are a few additional reasons that I would add to it. One is, I think the web, and this relates to your, our kind of excitement and enthusiasm about a world without borders that the web gave us. I do think that there are interesting innovations now that we're seeing.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Around democratic reinvention in non-contiguous, non-geographic environments as we form
 
 Beth S. Noveck: new versions of a health department, and new versions of governance in places that are… where we're reinventing the geographical borders, but I'll put that to one side for a moment. I think what the web gave us that we were so excited about is the ability to talk.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And we did not focus nearly enough on our ability to listen.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Number one. Number two, there was a huge amount of enthusiasm, energy, and passion from, the civic sector, from the nonprofit sector, from the research sector, around how do we make it easier for each of us to speak.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And we have not had nearly enough investment in your connection, that spine between the three pieces. So that first part about citizen participation
 
 Beth S. Noveck: how it connects to decision-making and implementation is not a place we've focused nearly enough, and I think we could get into a lot of structural reasons why we haven't done that, that has to do with education and technology, and where our focus has been, and the things we've chosen to study and to do, but we were so… I think we've been so giddy about the talking.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: that… and we were so excited at the time about, my gosh, we could each express ourselves. I mean, it was so… I think for people under a certain age who are here, who didn't live through the transition, the kind of birth of the World Wide Web, the recognition, like, it was so exciting that each of us had a megaphone.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Because we were coming from a world in which not only did we have 500 channels of TV and radio, but if you're over a certain age, you know, we had 4 channels of television, so the notion that suddenly each of us could have a blog, or, you know, I'm gonna date myself by naming some other platforms we used to yap on, like, that megaphone thing was so exciting, and then suddenly when you give everybody a megaphone.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Nobody can hear anymore. That's number one. Number two, I think that, lack of attention to decision-making, to how it connects up, which is why the two examples you gave at the outset of the work in Bowling Green and the work with Engaged California are both so exciting, because those address that last ten… that last mile problem, which is, how do I actually take all of this input
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And a lot of the examples we're going to talk about, and this is where AI comes in, is
 
 Beth S. Noveck: Is connecting that last mile back to institutions, and making it possible not only for institutions to hear and to listen with the scarce hours and attention that they have, but for each of us to hear one another in ways that were not possible before, when we were all talking.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And the last point I'll make, and this one is a little bit more controversial, and that's… and I'm gonna… I'm gonna make it and then push it back to you, is… comes back to your question… your point about why we engage.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: I think we've been particularly excited about this idea of legitimacy, which ties back to each of us having the ability, or not each of us, maybe a representative number of each of us, or some number of us, to speak.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And those arguments about what I would call collective intelligence, the information-gathering aspects.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: have really be… those are two siloed conversations. We have a world of democratic practitioners, sorry, practitioners, researchers, and others over here.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: We often have a collective intelligence or an open innovation community over here, and these worlds don't often talk to one another.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: And I think to our detriment, I think we have placed a lot of emphasis on how to do the legitimacy thing right, but not as much emphasis on how to do the collective intelligence or the decision-making piece right, and we've missed that kind of institutional hookup.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: So let me pause there and just push it back to you, because I think that in the Academy, we have sometimes done ourselves a disservice by not studying some of those second and third prongs that you've raised.
 
 Danielle Allen : Thanks, Beth.
 
 Beth S. Noveck: unfair.
 
 Danielle Allen : No, I think that's right. I would agree 100%, and what I would say, though, is
 
 Danielle Allen : I think the challenge is that part of hooking up the vertebrae is about using design principles for each vertebrae that get it ready to get hooked up. By that, I mean.
 
 Danielle Allen : So, in the civic participation space, I think you're right. We have focused on legitimacy, and so that means that probably the kind of overarching design principle people have focused on when they design citizen engagements is inclusion, right?
 
 Danielle Allen : who's participating? Are we opening up that town hall that only folks who don't work can come to because of the hours, and, you know, people with kids can't come to, and…
 
 Danielle Allen : Those kinds of questions. And inclusion matters, and AI can make that even stronger, especially with things like language access and the like. But the point is that there are other design principles that matter as well. And one of them is what, in 18th century vocabulary, people called energy.
 
 Danielle Allen : We could call it efficiency now. I mean, that is just plain the ability to actually get decisions done and get them through, and so that's where there can be a trade-off between inclusion, for example, and energy. And so I think… but if you're designing for both of those things when you design citizen engagement, then it actually means you're thinking about
 
 Danielle Allen : How does this set decision makers up to do their job? How does this set impleme
 
 [... truncated ...]
